x: personality rights aren't only for celebrities on 16 november, the madras high court restrained blinkit from using the persona of saravanan hari, the chennai super kings superfan, without his written consent. 📰 the facts • since around 2013, hari has appeared at csk matches with a yellow-painted face, curly wig, moustache, dhoni's no. 7 and a thumbs-up pose. it is widely covered on tv. • on 23 march 2025, a blinkit ad on the front page of the sunday times showed a cartoon figure with the same look and pose. • people he knew asked whether he was endorsing blinkit. pre-suit mediation failed, and he sued, claiming ₹1.1 crore. ⚖️ blinkit's defence: the characters were fictional and didn't resemble him. the court found a clear resemblance: the same pose was reproduced, and the public was likely to be misled into thinking it was him. 💬 the key line (justice p.b. balaji): "the constitution protects the rights of every individual and it need not be restricted or limited to celebrities like actors and sportspersons." blinkit could not exploit his personality rights, "whatever little it may be", for commercial gain without consent. 📌 relief (interim): no commercial use without written consent; the ad's artwork and emails must be preserved. the publisher's liability will be decided at trial. next hearing: 14 december. 🧭 where this fits in t. rangaraj (january 2026), the madras high court refused takedowns where posts merely circulated, insisting on commercial exploitation. hari's case applies the same test to a non-celebrity. read together, the test is identifiability plus commercial use without consent, not fame. 🔐 the privacy-law gap why not the dpdp act? ai training and copyright: three courts, three answers in ten days, courts in europe, canada and the us each moved on the same question: can an ai company train on copyrighted work without permission? 🇪🇺 european union (3 november) in like company v. google (c-250/25), advocate general szpunar said training is "as a rule, freely permitted" under the text-and-data-mining exception, if developers: • use only lawfully accessible sources • respect machine-readable opt-outs such as robots.txt • take steps to stop the model reproducing specific works but a chatbot fetching and reusing news in real time may still infringe press publishers' rights. 🇨🇦 canada (13 november) the ontario court of appeal unanimously held that openai must defend the canadian news publishers' suit in ontario. openai argued that its training happened outside the province. the court found "a real and substantial connection". canadian fair dealing, not us fair use, will apply, and there is no text-and-data-mining exception. this decides venue only. 🇺🇸 united states (pending) in in re openai copyright infringement litigation, judge sidney stein will decide fair use on cross-motions for summary judgment, without a trial. on 6 november he allowed 56 amicus briefs. 🇮🇳 and india? in ani v. openai, the delhi high court (24 july) kept jurisdiction, held training-related storage prima facie covered by section 52(1)(a)(i), and refused an interim injunction. ani's appeal is pending. indonesia is legislating instead, and google, meta and tiktok opposed its bill on 11 november. three patterns across the courts: 1️⃣ location isn't a shield. delhi and ontario both rejected "we trained abroad". 2️⃣ opt-outs matter. the eu makes them the line, and the delhi hc weighed the unused crawler opt-out against ani. 3️⃣ outputs are the weak point. regurgitation is where liability sits. my take: india shouldn't leave this to one interim order. stretching "private use, including research" to cover commercial ai training is a fragile base for a whole industry. a clear statutory rule with opt-outs, transparency and anti-memorisation duties would serve creators and developers better. 📎 resources: • cjeu press release: https://curia.europa.eu/site/jcms/p1_1000088855 • ctv on ontario: https://ctvnews.ca/sci-tech/article/court-allows-news-publishers-copyright-lawsuit-against-openai-to-go-ahead • ipwatchdog on the us briefs: https://ipwatchdog.com/2026/11/02/openai-touts-briefs-backing-fair-use-for-ai-training/ • livelaw on ani: https://www.livelaw.in/high-court/delhi-high-court/delhi-high-court-rejects-ani-copyright-suit-open-ai-chatgpt-542736 which approach should india take: fair dealing, an opt-out exception, or licensing? hyderabad police now has an ai that maps "criminal networks". which law tells it where to stop? on 12 november, commissioner v.c. sajjanar launched dooradrishti, an ai platform built in-house by hyderabad city police. it compiles profiles of accused persons, analyses their activities and identifies links between individuals and criminal networks, using police databases and data from other departments. the stated aim: faster evidence, faster charge sheets, and a shift "from reactive to proactive policing". organised crime and cyber fraud do run through networks, so the aim is legitimate. but five questions haven't been answered publicly: 1️⃣ does it include people never convicted, or acquitted? 2️⃣ how does it make links, and how are false links caught? 3️⃣ does it reach beyond criminal records, to movements or activity? 4️⃣ who can access it, for how long, and is it audited? 5️⃣ must officers verify its findings before acting? the legal frame: 🔹 puttaswamy: state intrusion on privacy needs a law, a legitimate aim, proportionality and safeguards 🔹 dpdp act s. 17: processing to prevent, detect or investigate offences is largely exempt (from may 2027) 🔹 malak singh (1981): police surveillance registers must be limited to people reasonably suspected 🔹 criminal procedure (identification) act, 2022: records of people never convicted must be destroyed on release, discharge or acquittal and telangana has been here before. in 2022, the high court issued notice in s.q. masood's pil, india's first court challenge to police facial recognition without a law. the risk with network mapping is guilt by link: a relative, neighbour or client flagged by association, old firs and acquittals that never leave the system, and no way to know or correct your profile. being linked to someone isn't evidence of a crime. my take: six safeguards before scale (slide 7): ✔ a published legal basis and sop ✔ scope limited to charge-sheeted and convicted persons, for specific cases ✔ human verification: ai output is a lead, never evidence on its own ✔ deletion for the acquitted and discharged ✔ logs and independent audits of every search ✔ a right to know and correct one's profile, with an annual transparency report hyderabad can lead on ai policing. it should also lead on the rules. 📎 resources: • medianama: https://lnkd.in/d-ichntj • newsmeter: https://lnkd.in/dzfxf2uc what safeguard would you want first? can a privacy law quietly weaken the right to information? the supreme court hears that question again on 17 november. last month i wrote about the news publishers' challenge to the dpdp act. but the larger case, venkatesh nayak v. union of india, goes well beyond journalism. rti activist venkatesh nayak, ncpri, the reporters' collective and nitin sethi filed in february. the court issued notice, refused an interim stay and referred the matter to a larger bench. the publishers' plea (dnpa) joined in october. the central challenge is s. 44(3), which rewrote rti s. 8(1)(j): 🔹 before: personal information was exempt only if unrelated to public activity or an unwarranted invasion of privacy, and could be disclosed if a larger public interest justified it 🔹 after: "information which relates to personal information" is exempt, full stop 🔹 the clause's own public-interest test is gone, and so is the proviso that what can't be denied to parliament can't be denied to a citizen why rti users worry: officials' assets and qualifications, welfare beneficiary lists used in social audits, contractor payments and recruitment records can all now be refused as "personal information". five more provisions are under challenge: 1️⃣ s. 17: wide exemptions for state agencies 2️⃣ s. 36 with rule 23(2): the centre can demand data from any fiduciary, and the person may not be told 3️⃣ s. 18 with rule 17: board members chosen by an executive-led committee 4️⃣ s. 33(1): penalties for a "significant" breach, a term the act doesn't define 5️⃣ no journalism exemption (the publishers' plea) both sides have a case. petitioners call it a "sledgehammer" where a "chisel" was needed, relying on subhash chandra agarwal (2019). defenders point to puttaswamy, to rti misuse in private disputes, and to s. 8(2), which still allows disclosure where public interest outweighs harm. the cji said "some ironing out of the creases" might be needed. my take: privacy and transparency aren't opposites. restore a public-interest test inside s. 8(1)(j), at least for public functionaries, and bring back the parliament proviso. put independent oversight on s. 36 demands, and make the board truly independent. what to watch on 17 november: the union's reply, whether a larger bench is constituted, and a timeline before may 2027, when most of the act's duties begin. 📎 resources: • supreme court observer case (purchase records show procurement, not confirmed use on anyone.) the legal gap: 🔹 bnss ss. 105–106 cover search, seizure and video recording, not unlocking or copying a phone 🔹 it act s. 69 needs a written home secretary order to decrypt, and has been under challenge in the supreme court since 2019 🔹 bsa s. 63 certifies electronic records for court; it doesn't make the extraction lawful 🔹 dpdp act s. 17 exempts processing for investigation (from may 2027) 🔹 guidelines on seizing digital devices, promised to the supreme court in 2023, still haven't been placed before it under puttaswamy, any intrusion on privacy needs a law, a legitimate aim and proportionality. investigating crime is a legitimate aim. but there's no specific law, and full extraction copies far more than any offence needs. if your phone is seized (slide 6): ✔ get the seizure memo listing the device ✔ ask that the hash value be recorded at seizure ✔ take legal advice before giving passwords; the law on compelled passwords is unsettled ✔ lawyers and journalists: flag privileged and source material in writing ✔ apply for return of the device (bnss s. 497) and deletion of copied data if you're not charged my take: investigators need these tools, but the rules should come before the purchase orders. a judicial warrant for extraction, scope limited to the offence, a log of every extraction, deletion when no charge is filed, independent audits, and extra protection for lawyers and journalists. 📎 resources: • medianama: https://lnkd.in/dmhvsfwf • internet freedom foundation: https://lnkd.in/damuxmxy should police need a judge's warrant before copying your phone? views are personal; for general information only. privacy dataprotection surveillance digitalrights puttaswamy criminallaw bnss technologylaw legalupdate

a cartoon exaggerates. a deepfake convinces. where does political satire end? the delhi high court gave an early answer on 6 november in rekha gupta v. aam aadmi party & ors. (justice manoj jain). the delhi chief minister sued over ai-generated videos and images posted from the party's verified accounts, allegedly showing her as a liquor vendor serving drinks and as head of a "ghar ghar theka" scheme. the court described the visuals as a "near-perfect imitation." what the court said: 🔹 public figures must accept criticism and political humour, and parties remain free to attack government policies 🔹 but there is a "thin line": satire "cannot be permitted to create irreparable wound on someone's dignity" 🔹 ai makes realistic fakes easy, but responsibility for making and posting them stays with humans 🔹 content that spreads fast on social media risks irreparable harm it ordered six urls taken down immediately and listed the case for 4 december. this is an interim order; the defendants' case is yet to be heard. why ai changes the satire question: satire works because the audience knows it isn't real. a cartoon or mimicry is obviously exaggeration. a realistic ai video can pass as real, and once shared without context, the joke disappears and only the false impression remains. the legal frame: article 19(1)(a) protects satire; article 19(2) permits restrictions for defamation. civil suits, criminal defamation (bns s. 356), the february 2026 it rules on labelling synthetic content, and election commission advisories on deepfakes all apply. my take, a five-question test: 1️⃣ would a reasonable viewer know it isn't real? 2️⃣ is it clearly labelled as ai-generated or parody, on the content itself? 3️⃣ does it target a policy, or fabricate conduct by a person? 4️⃣ who posted it? an official party account carries more responsibility 5️⃣ would it be acceptable as a cartoon? instagram blocked your account. can you go straight to the high court? the delhi high court says no, at least not by writ. in sarthak bhagat v. union of india (order dated 27 october), justice amit mahajan dealt with a user whose instagram accounts were disabled without notice or specific reasons. the in-app review failed, and his appeal to the grievance appellate committee (gac) went undecided past its 30-day deadline. the court held: 🔹 a writ under article 226 isn't maintainable against meta. it doesn't perform a public function or discharge a public duty 🔹 instagram shapes public opinion, but that's a consequence of the platform, not a duty it owes. its operations "remain private in nature" 🔹 restoration has to be sought through a civil suit 🔹 the gac was directed to decide his appeal quickly the catch: the gac is jammed. as of 22 september, 49,978 of 63,353 appeals were pending, about four in five. how it fits with three other high court rulings in six weeks: • mp hc (anmol jain, 17 sept): platforms can act on infringing content; gac is an adequate safeguard • p&h hc (reported 20 oct): government-ordered blocks can be challenged by writ • bombay hc (meta v. blink digital, 27 oct): indian civil courts can hear it rules claims, despite meta's california clause • delhi hc (27 oct): no writ for meta's own decisions so the first question is: who blocked you? take: a caste label on the first page of a case does real damage. 1️⃣ it erodes the image of an unbiased system. a court that labels litigants by caste signals that identity matters, even when it a "digital arrest" victim sends the money themselves. until now, that meant the bank could say: not our problem. the supreme court has just changed that conversation. on 29 october, a bench of cji surya kant, justice joymalya bagchi and justice v. mohana, hearing the suo motu case on digital arrest scams, told the rbi that its new rules must include a liability clause: 🔹 banks must compensate victims where inadequate safeguards or a failure of due diligence contributed to the fraud 🔹 compensation of not less than the amount the customer lost 🔹 the bank pays, not just the employee involved ("the bank will have to pay," said the cji) 🔹 safeguards to consider: temporarily holding transactions out of line with an account's history, automatic alerts to police, and verification before release why this matters: the rbi's 2017 circular gives zero liability for "unauthorised" transactions where the bank is at fault. but in a digital arrest, the victim authorises the transfer, under fear and deception. so victims have often fallen outside it, even when the bank let sudden, unusual transfers through without a single check. what's next: the rbi has proposed notifying its kyc amendment directions by 30 november (also the next hearing) and bringing them into force by 31 december. separately, a draft would let banks flag and hold suspected mule-account transactions, and the government has proposed a one-hour delay on payments of ₹10,000 or more. my take: five questions the final rules must answer. 1️⃣ who decides that due diligence failed? not the bank alone; the burden should stay on the bank, as in 2017 2️⃣ what counts as due diligence? clear triggers: large first-time transfers, new payees, elderly or dormant accounts 3️⃣ how fast is the refund? a provisional credit within days, not years of litigation 4️⃣ who is covered? nbfcs, wallets and payment apps too 5️⃣ what about genuine payments? holds need short time limits and a quick release route if you get the call: no indian agency arrests anyone over a video call, and no genuine officer asks you to transfer money to "verify" it. if you've already paid, call 1930 or report at cybercrime.gov.in immediately, tell your bank in writing, file an fir, and escalate to the rbi ombudsman if needed (slide 7). please share this with your parents and grandparents. they're the most frequent targets. 📎 resources: • business standard: https://lnkd.in/dcvh2qjq • medianama: https://lnkd.in/d7btemea • report cyber fraud: https://cybercrime.gov.in should banks bear the loss when their systems miss an obvious red flag? can a privacy law stop journalists from doing their job? india's biggest media houses have asked the supreme court. reuters reported on 26 october that 21 news publishers, acting through the digital news publishers association (dnpa), have challenged the digital personal data protection act. dnpa members include network18, ndtv, the indian express and times internet. the case is listed for hearing on 27 october. they want key provisions struck down before they take effect in may 2027. their four concerns: 🔹 notice and consent (ss. 5–6): journalists may need consent from the very people they investigate 🔹 erasure (ss. 8(7), 12): withdrawal of consent and erasure with no public-interest safeguard could force stories off the record 🔹 information demands (s. 36 with rule 23): the centre can call for information from any data fiduciary, risking exposure of sources 🔹 blocking (s. 37): access can be blocked "in the interests of the general public" underneath it all: there is no exemption for journalism. the 2018 draft, the 2019 bill and the 2021 jpc version all had one. it was dropped in 2022. the state gets wide exemptions under s. 17; the press gets none. the government's position: in july 2025, meity told media bodies no exemption was needed, said journalists aren't data fiduciaries, and offered faqs. separate petitions by venkatesh nayak, the reporters' collective and ncpri (on the rti amendment and s. 36) were referred to a larger bench in february 2026, without a stay. today, a journalist's only clear relief is s. 3(c)(ii): data the person (or a legal duty) made public falls outside the act. most investigative material doesn't fit. my take: fix it, don't scrap it. 1️⃣ put the exemption in the law; an faq can't override the text 2️⃣ base it on purpose (journalism in the public interest), not status, so freelancers are covered 3️⃣ keep security and breach duties; newsrooms hold sensitive data too 4️⃣ require independent or judicial approval before s. 36 demands reach journalistic material 5️⃣ apply a public-interest test before published reports or archives are erased the eu, uk and singapore all build this balance in (slide 5). newsroom checklist on slide 7: subscriber and employee data is covered whatever the court decides. 📎 resources: • reuters report (via wtvb): https://lnkd.in/dugfm4bu • sc notice on the earlier petitions (the wire): https://lnkd.in/dvqz9bdr • meity–media meeting (the tech trace): https://lnkd.in/djkpitie should india's privacy law have a journalism exemption? views are personal; the keys that secure the internet are supposed to take billions of years to guess. an ai agent guessed these in one prompt. what happened: emudhra, a licensed indian certificate authority (ca), published eight intermediate certificate keys in april 2025. because of a faulty step in its key-generation ceremony, each private key was a number below 256. trying 256 values was enough to recover them. security researcher scott helme said he recovered all eight in under a second, and that an ai agent did the same from a single prompt. the flaw went unnoticed for about 18 months, through two audit cycles. once a researcher reported it on 17 october, mozilla and chrome blocked the certificates the same day, apple and microsoft followed, and emudhra revoked all eight. emudhra says it has found no evidence of misuse, that only one us customer ecosystem was affected, and that its indian digital signature and esign services run on separate systems and are unaffected. why lawyers should care: a ca is a digital notary. whoever holds its private key can forge trusted certificates, impersonate websites and intercept encrypted traffic. what the it act says (chapter vi): 🔹 section 30: a ca must use hardware, software and procedures secure from intrusion and misuse 🔹 section 34(2): if an event affects the integrity of its systems, it must use reasonable efforts to notify those likely to be affected 🔹 section 25: the controller of certifying authorities (cca) can suspend or revoke a licence for failing to maintain section 30 procedures the questions this raises (my take): 1️⃣ two regimes: the it act licenses cas for electronic signature certificates; website certificates are policed mainly by browser root programs. do section 30 duties reach a licensed ca's global tls business? that's untested. 2️⃣ the weak keys passed two audits. what were the auditors checking? 3️⃣ who compensates relying parties? section 43a covers only sensitive personal data, and dpdp security duties start in may 2027. for now, remedies sit mostly in contracts and their liability caps. the contrast is striking: four foreign browser makers acted within 72 hours. as of 21 october, the cca had made no public statement, though meity officials said a team was investigating. 📎 resources: • medianama explainer: https://lnkd.in/durty7wz • bleepingcomputer: https://lnkd.in/dxpzpe8c • emudhra's statement: https://lnkd.in/dkc_dn84 should india's ca rules be rewritten for the ai era? should children be kept off the internet to keep them safe? the supreme court has said no. in just rights for children alliance v. s. harish (order dated 15 october 2026, pardiwala & chandran, jj.), the court held that internet access is a fundamental right for every individual, children included, under article 21 read with article 19(1)(a). its reasoning in one line: "to keep the child away from the internet on account of such failures would be to mistake the victim for the problem." key holdings: 🔹 blanket, age-based bans are disproportionate. they may push children to unregulated platforms and make them less likely to report abuse 🔹 checking every user's age carries its own risk of sensitive data collection and surveillance 🔹 protection should target the harm: those who make, share or sell child sexual exploitation and abuse material (cseam), and platforms that fail to remove it 🔹 platforms that ignore pocso and it rules duties cannot rely on safe harbour under section 79 what the court wants instead: ✔ a "child mode": private by default, limited contact from unknown adults, moderated ads and content ✔ a national hash & url list database for cseam, with at least three trained human analysts making the final assessment ✔ immediate removal of content that matches the database ✔ reporting within two steps, acknowledgement within 24 hours, and final decisions by trained humans, not algorithms ✔ exemplary fines scaled to a platform's size and turnover, and forfeiture of revenue earned from such content behind paywalls ✔ digital safety education in schools and free counselling for victims the centre must report progress by the next hearing on 10 december 2026. my take: the dpdp angle (slide 7) section 9 of the dpdp act requires verifiable parental consent before processing data of anyone under 18, and bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted ads aimed at children, from 13 may 2027. but verifying consent means knowing who is a child, and the court has warned that checking everyone's age is itself a privacy risk. platforms will need age checks that collect as little data as possible. the burden has shifted from children to platforms. 📎 two words changed in india's data protection law this month. here's why they matter. on 5 october 2026, meity issued the digital personal data protection (removal of difficulties) order, 2026 under section 43(1) of the dpdp act. it was published in the gazette on 7 october. the changes are small, but both affect how compliance programmes are written: 1️⃣ section 9(1): children and persons with disability the text now reads "personal data of a child or of a person with disability". the added "of" makes the two categories parallel and independent. verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian is still required, exactly as before. 2️⃣ section 10(2)(c)(ii): significant data fiduciaries "periodic audit" becomes "periodic data audit". the sdf audit is about data protection compliance, not a general audit, and audit charters and auditor engagements should say so. what has not changed: • no new obligations are created • the ban on tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising aimed at children stays • penalties of up to ₹200 crore (children's data) and ₹150 crore (sdf duties) remain sections 9 and 10 commence on 13 may 2027 under the november 2025 commencement notification. for ed-tech platforms, schools, health apps and large platforms, this order is a useful prompt to: • align consent notices and privacy policies with the clarified wording • map every flow of children's and pwd data and test verifiable-consent journeys • re-label sdf audit scopes and engagement letters as "data audit" i've summarised the changes, timeline and a short checklist in the attached slides. 📚 resources: • official gazette of india (notifications): https://egazette.gov.in • summary of the order (india briefing): https://lnkd.in/dveq76-z • dpdp rules commencement timeline (g.s.r. 843(e)): https://lnkd.in/dmjuk5n6 views are personal and for general information only. dpdp dataprotection privacy dataprivacy dpdpact childrensprivacy compliance technologylaw indialaw

can an ai company train on indian news without permission? in ani media pvt. ltd. v. open ai opco llc, cs(comm) 1028/2024, the delhi high court has given india its first answer, at least for now. on 24 july 2026, justice amit bansal dismissed ani's application for an interim injunction (i.a. 45300/2024). the key takeaways: 1️⃣ jurisdiction (paras 48–55): storing ani's works on us servers is only the "terminal step in the chain of events" that begins with accessing them from india. moving servers abroad cannot be used to evade indian copyright law. 2️⃣ storage is reproduction (paras 145–151): under section 14(a)(i), storing a work "in any medium by electronic means", temporarily or permanently, is reproduction. but section 14 operates "subject to the provisions of this act", so an act covered by section 52 is not infringement. 3️⃣ fair dealing under section 52(1)(a)(i) (paras 190–255): • commercial use alone does not exclude the defence (para 190) • "private" is not limited to individuals and can cover a company using data in a closed space (paras 208–211) • "research" gets an updating construction and extends to machine learning (para 218) • instead of the us four-factor test, the court applied a purpose test and a fairness test: no market substitution of ani's news feed was shown, and the public interest in llms was established (paras 234–255) 4️⃣ outputs (para 271): chatgpt's outputs, including those generated using rag, were prima facie not substantially similar to ani's works, and ani failed to show memorisation or regurgitation. the 14 articles relied on were published after the models' training cut-offs. 5️⃣ balance of convenience (paras 262–270): ani had not used the available opt-out to block openai's crawlers, and an injunction would harm the public at large. what it leaves open: • will this broad reading of "private use, including research" survive appeal or the final hearing? the court itself notes its observations have no bearing on the outcome of the suit (para 274). • how does it sit alongside gema v. openai in germany and thomson reuters v. ross in the us third circuit, which went the other way on their facts?
